name: Warm compress / meibomian care

card.summary: Heating the eyelids to loosen oil blockages in the meibomian glands, a standard first step for blepharitis and evaporative dry eye with a modest research base.
card.aka: Warm eyelid compress, lid hygiene, eyelid heat therapy
card.note: Compress temperature and method vary widely; burns are possible with excess heat.

quick.overview:
Warm compresses are cloth, gel or device-delivered heat applied to closed eyelids to soften thickened oil in the meibomian glands, which line the lid edges and supply the tear film's oily layer. They are a conservative first-line measure for meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD), blepharitis and evaporative dry eye.

In appearance circles they are discussed for puffy, red or irritated lids and for lash-line health. The research concerns tear quality and gland function, not cosmetic outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Heat is thought to melt thickened meibum so it can flow out of blocked glands. A study of 20 dry eye patients measured tear-film lipid layer thickness after 5, 15 and 30 minutes of warm moist compress therapy.
quick.risks: Encyclopedic guidance gives a safe range of roughly 40 to 45 degrees Celsius and warns that higher heat can burn tissue and that people with reduced sensation need extra care. Studies of home methods note that heat delivered to the inner eyelid depends heavily on how the compress is made.

lead: A warm compress applies moist or dry heat, commonly through a heated cloth, gel mask or electric device, to the closed eyelids. It is a long-standing conservative treatment for meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD), the leading cause of evaporative dry eye, which is marked by blocked gland ducts and altered oil secretion that destabilise the tear film [1][2].

Eyelid warming is combined in practice with lid hygiene and sometimes gland expression, and is compared in trials with in-office devices such as LipiFlow [3]. Reviews state that there is no single gold-standard treatment for MGD and that options range from conservative measures to procedures [1][4].
Studies show warming can change tear lipid layer thickness [5] and that home methods differ in how much heat they deliver [6].
infobox: Home or clinic heat therapy for eyelids

paras: Compresses may be moist (a warm wet cloth) or dry (microwavable packs, eye masks), and commercial devices aim to hold temperature steadily. Encyclopedic sources describe a therapeutic range of roughly 40 to 45 degrees Celsius and warn that higher temperatures risk burns [7].

Blepharitis, an inflammation of the lid margins, is common but has been described as poorly defined, with limited data on prevalence and how practitioners treat it. A survey-based 2009 study of US adults examined its frequency and treatment [8].

In a study of 20 dry eye patients with MGD, tear-film lipid layer thickness was measured after 5, 15 and 30 minutes of warm moist compress therapy [5]. A study of inner eyelid surface temperature found that the method of making a compress influenced the heat reaching the lid [6]. A warm moist air device was evaluated for tear function in simple MGD [9].

A 12-month report on a single vectored thermal pulsation treatment described sustained effects on MGD and evaporative dry eye [10]. A randomised open-label crossover trial with 139 subjects compared LipiFlow with an iHeat warm compress in MGD [3]. A 2020 review summarised evidence-based treatments for MGD [4]. A consensus-style report on the digital environment's effect on the ocular surface also covers eyelid and tear-film changes related to screen use [11].
Encyclopedic guidance advises testing compress warmth, avoiding use on open wounds or numb areas, and seeking care if symptoms worsen [7]. Overheating can cause burns.

Human studies include the tear lipid layer study [5], inner eyelid temperature measurements [6], a warm moist air device study [9], a randomised trial against a thermal pulsation device [3] and a 12-month follow-up of that technology [10]. No studies found tested warm compresses for cosmetic eyelid appearance.

timeline.event: Study measures tear lipid layer thickness after warm moist compresses in MGD patients [5].
Randomised trial compares LipiFlow with warm compress in MGD [3].
